documents.title: IWGDF guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetic foot disease

chunks.content: Introduction Infected bone defects are common and serious complications following trauma, osteomyelitis, and revision surgeries, particularly when large bone defects of the limbs are accompanied by soft tissue damage [ ]. These bone defects often lead to recurrent infections due to the loss of mechanical support, persistent infection, and insufficient soft tissue coverage [ ]. Traditional treatments such as autologous bone grafting, the Masquelet technique, and Ilizarov bone transport face challenges such as long treatment cycles, a high incidence of complications (with infection recurrence rates ranging from 15% to 30%), and limited functional recovery [ – ]. In recent years, 3D-printed customized titanium alloy prostheses have provided a new direction for bone defect reconstruction after infection control, thanks to their advantages in precise anatomical matching, immediate mechanical stability, and microporous structure that promotes bone ingrowth [ , ]. The clinical application of 3D-printed microporous titanium in orthopedics initially began with the repair and reconstruction after bone tumor resection and limb-salvage surgeries, achieving favorable results [ ]. In osteomyelitis treatment, given the complexity and high cost of traditional Masquelet and Ilizarov bone transport techniques, personalized 3D printing technology can promote bone-prosthesis interface integration and bone ingrowth through porosity, while maintaining good mechanical support [ ]. Furthermore, soft tissue defects associated with complex cases remain a key factor limiting their effectiveness. The lack of well-vascularized soft tissue coverage significantly increases the risk of prosthesis exposure and recurrent infection [ ]. For the repair of soft tissue defects of varying degrees, free flap techniques (such as the anterolateral thigh free flap) can effectively reduce dead space, promote wound healing, and reduce the risk of deep infection by providing well-vascularized tissue coverage [ , ]. Current research on the treatment of infected bone defects primarily focuses on single treatment strategies, such as prosthesis implantation or local pedicled flap repair. For example, Liu et al. [ ] reported on the use of 3D-printed microporous titanium implants for treating infected bone defects caused by osteomyelitis, with 6 out of 8 patients achieving good bone integration. We also reported the use of single microporous titanium prosthesis implantation for treating 18 patients with infected bone defects caused by osteomyelitis, with 17 patients (94.4%) achieving good healing [ ]. Previously, in 2022, we first reported the preliminary efficacy of free/local flaps combined with 3D-printed microporous titanium for treating 6 cases of lower limb infected bone defects with soft tissue loss, with 5 patients achieving good wound healing (83.3%) [ ]. Additionally, Chen et al. [ ] used local transposition flaps combined with 3D-printed microporous titanium to treat 13 patients with femoral bone defects following osteomyelitis, achieving good bone integration and wound healing in 7 cases during follow-up. However, the personalized harvesting of free flaps and the advantages of covering large soft tissue defects are not addressed in existing studies. On the other hand, current research is limited to lower limb cases, with a lack of evidence for the efficacy in upper limb infected bone defects. Importantly, these clinical efficacy and safety data have not been validated in large-scale studies. The biomechanical performance of the 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis has been systematically evaluated in our previous study using integrated biomechanical testing and finite element analysis, which demonstrated sufficient load-bearing capacity, favorable stress distribution, and resistance to fatigue failure [ ]. Building on this biomechanical foundation, we conducted the largest single-center retrospective cohort study to date to evaluate the clinical safety and effectiveness of a staged reconstructive strategy incorporating personalized 3D-printed microporous titanium prostheses for infected bone defects. This strategy integrates individualized prosthesis implantation with free flap reconstruction when required, allowing its application to infected bone defects with varying degrees of soft tissue involvement at different anatomical locations in the limbs (Fig. ). In addition to assessing overall clinical outcomes, we explored risk factors associated with postoperative complications. Patients were further stratified into subgroups according to the presence or absence of significant soft tissue defects, namely a single prosthesis group and a combined free flap group. Rather than aiming to compare these subgroups for superiority, subgroup analyses were performed to characterize clinical features and recovery trajectories across different tiers of reconstructive complexity, thereby evaluating the applicability and universality of the staged treatment protocol. The staged approach consisted of: (1) infection control with or without individualized free flap coverage based on soft tissue requirements; and (2) definitive bone reconstruction using a customized 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis. Materials and methods Study design This is a retrospective study. Our institution specializes in the treatment of infected bone defects caused by various factors and has extensive experience in limb repair and reconstruction. After approval from the institutional ethics review board (2019-018-02), we conducted a retrospective data collection and analysis of a series of patients who underwent microporous titanium implant treatment from January 2019 to January 2025. This cohort study has been reported in line with the STROCSS guidelines [ , ]. Patient selection The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) For bone defect characteristics, patients with infected nonunion or traumatic bone defects in the limbs (including tibia, femur, humerus, radius, carpal bones, metacarpal bones, and metatarsal bones, etc.) where the bone defect length after debridement could not be repaired by traditional autologous or artificial bone grafts (confirmed by imaging measurements and 3D CT reconstruction); (2) Patients with concomitant soft tissue defects that could not be closed by direct suturing or skin grafting (evaluated by wound measurement software or intraoperative sterile film method); (3) Postoperative follow-up ≥ 3 months with complete imaging (X-ray/CT) and laboratory data. Additionally, the study excluded the following: (1) Severe uncontrolled underlying diseases (such as uncontrolled diabetes: HbA1c > 8%, heart failure grade III-IV, cirrhosis Child-Pugh class C) (2), Long-term use of immunosuppressants or corticosteroids (prednisone ≥ 10 mg/d, continuous use for > 3 months); (3) Tumor-related bone destruction (primary bone tumors or metastatic tumors), radiation-induced bone necrosis, congenital skeletal deformities; (4) Loss to follow-up or missing critical data (imaging, functional scores). All surgeries were performed by the same senior surgeon to reduce heterogeneity in the procedure. Surgical technique and postoperative rehabilitation This study employed a two-stage surgical approach to treat complex infected bone defects. Prior to the second surgery, a 3D CT scan was used to assess the morphology of the bone defect and the extent of soft tissue involvement, after which an individualized 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis was custom-designed (pore diameter 700–750 μm, porosity 65–75%). The first-stage surgery involved thorough debridement, removal of necrotic bone and soft tissue, and the implantation of vancomycin-loaded bone cement (2 g vancomycin/40 g bone cement). Simultaneously, a free anterolateral thigh flap was used to repair the concomitant soft tissue defect in 25 cases. Postoperatively, antibiotic treatment based on bacterial culture results was administered until the infection was completely controlled (CRP, ESR, and white blood cell counts normalized for two consecutive tests). In the second-stage surgery, the induced membrane was preserved, bone cement was removed, and the pre-designed microporous titanium prosthesis was implanted (secured by intramedullary protrusion anchor and titanium plate fixation). The surface of the prosthesis was coated with vancomycin sulfate calcium. Regardless of whether the procedure involved a single implantation or a combined free flap repair, all patients received standardized nursing and rehabilitation. Detailed information regarding staged surgery and postoperative rehabilitation can be found in Supplemental Material 1, including first-stage surgery, postoperative management, design and manufacturing of 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis, and second-stage surgery and postoperative rehabilitation. Data collection and outcome measures Outpatient follow-up and data collection were performed at baseline and at 3, 6, and 12 months postoperatively, with annual reviews thereafter. All follow-up data were collected and organized by research assistants, and electronic medical records were reviewed, including case files, surgical details, laboratory, and imaging data. The baseline data obtained for patients included age, gender, and medical history; primary characteristics included etiology (traumatic or non-traumatic) of the bone defect, location, length, soft tissue defect area, flap type, and bacterial culture results. Laboratory and imaging assessments (X-ray and CT) were performed preoperatively and at 3, 6, and 12 months postoperatively, with subsequent annual checks. Visual analogue scale (VAS) scores [ ] were recorded at each follow-up. CRP and ESR were measured at each follow-up time point, and infection control was considered achieved if the values normalized for two consecutive tests (CRP < 10 mg/L, ESR < 20 mm/h). Additionally, implant integration and stability were evaluated using X-ray and CT examinations. Successful implant integration was defined by fulfillment of all of the following criteria: (1) progressive trabecular bone formation at the bone–prosthesis interface; (2) absence of progressive radiolucent lines greater than 2 mm; and (3) absence of implant migration, loosening, or mechanical failure. Failure to meet any one of these criteria was classified as poor implant integration. For lower limb cases, postoperative functional recovery was assessed using the Lower Extremity Functional Scale (LEFS) [ ], recording the postoperative standing time, walking time with crutches, and time to full weight-bearing. Clinical signs included the absence of sinus tract, persistent drainage, local erythema, swelling, or pain. Additionally, pre-defined complications included wound recurrent infection, flap necrosis, poor wound healing, prosthesis-related infections, prosthesis-related fractures, implant fractures, and non-union. Statistical analysis Data analysis was performed using IBM SPSS (version 29.0). For baseline data, continuous variables were presented as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range) and categorical variables were expressed as frequency (percentage). Differences in LEFS and VAS scores before and after surgery were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Predefined complications (such as recurrent infection, prosthesis fracture, etc.) were treated as binary outcome variables. Univariate logistic regression was performed to assess the relationship between patients’ baseline characteristics (age, gender, bone defect length, etc.) and surgical features (flap repair, bacterial type, etc.). Odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Baseline characteristics From February 2019 to January 2025, 82 patients with osteomyelitis caused by trauma or non-trauma underwent staged surgeries. All patients signed an informed consent form for surgery. Two patients were excluded because they did not undergo the second-stage surgery after the first debridement and vancomycin-loaded implant. In the end, 80 patients met the eligibility criteria and were included in the analysis. Among these, 54 were male (67.5%) and 26 were female (32.5%), with an average age of 47.5 ± 9.3 years, an average BMI of 26.6 ± 2.9 kg/m², and an average follow-up time of 40.8 ± 14.8 months. The majority of infected bone defects were traumatic (52 cases, 65%). There were 24 patients with a history of hypertension, 10 with a history of diabetes, and 4 with both hypertension and diabetes. The median bone defect length was 11.4 cm (range 3.8–32.0 cm), and the soft tissue defect area ranged from approximately 5.0 × 8.0 cm to 33 × 10 cm (Table ). None of the 80 patients lost to follow-up at the last visit. Among the 55 cases in the single microporous titanium implant group, 37 were male (69.1%) and 18 were female (30.9%), with an average age of 47.0 ± 7.8 years and an average follow-up time of 42.8 ± 12.3 months. The range of soft tissue defect area was approximately 5.0 cm × 8.0 cm to 33 cm × 10 cm. The median bone defect length was 10.5 cm (range 3.5–28.0 cm), including 32 cases of tibial bone defects, 11 cases of femoral bone defects, 5 cases of humeral bone defects, 4 cases of radial bone defects, and 3 cases of combined carpal and metacarpal bone defects. In the free flap combined group, there were 25 cases, with 17 males (68.0%) and 8 females (32.0%), with an average age of 48.5 ± 12.1 years and an average follow-up time of 36.4 ± 15.5 months. The median bone defect length was 12.0 cm (range 3.8–32.0 cm), including 3 cases with extensive dorsal foot soft tissue defects accompanied by large segments of metatarsal bone defects, 19 cases with lower leg soft tissue defects accompanied by large segments of tibial bone defects, and 3 cases of hand and forearm soft tissue defects combined with metacarpal and carpal bone defects. Gram-negative (G⁻) infections accounted for 16% (4/25), all due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Mixed infections ( Staphylococcus aureus + Pseudomonas aeruginosa ) accounted for 8% (2/25). Complications A total of 8 complications occurred during the postoperative follow-up period among 80 patients, resulting in an overall complication rate of 10% (Table ). The complications were categorized as recurrent infections and prosthesis fractures, occurring at an average of 7.5 ± 3.6 months postoperatively. Among these, recurrent infection was the most common complication (7.5%), occurring at an average of 5.8 ± 3.1 months postoperatively. Prosthesis fracture occurred in 2.5% of cases, with an average onset at 11.5 months postoperatively. Notably, the tibia was the most common site of complications, accounting for 50% of all complications. Specifically, in the single 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis group, two patients experienced recurrent tibial infections at 6 and 11 months postoperatively. After debridement, vancomycin-loaded bone cement was implanted, and both patients resumed walking at 6- and 8-months post second-stage surgery, respectively. One patient developed a recurrent infection at 5 months postoperatively, and after debridement and implantation of vancomycin-loaded bone cement, walking was restored 6 months post second-stage surgery. Another patient in the same group experienced a femoral prosthesis fracture at 13 months postoperatively, which was followed by prosthesis removal and implantation of vancomycin-loaded bone cement, with walking restored 7 months after the second-stage surgery. In the free flap combined treatment group, two diabetic patients developed foot wound infections at 3 and 4 months postoperatively. Both patients underwent prosthesis removal and replacement with vancomycin-loaded bone cement, with walking restored at 5- and 7-months post second-stage surgery, respectively. In the free flap combined treatment group, two diabetic patients developed foot wound infections at 3 and 4 months postoperatively. Another patient had a tibial fixation prosthesis screw fracture at 10 months postoperatively. After revision surgery, walking was restored 5 months later, with no recurrence of infection observed. Risk factors of complications Exploratory risk factor analysis ( Table ) showed that diabetes mellitus was associated with a higher occurrence of postoperative complications in both univariate logistic regression (OR = 11; p = 0.004) and Fisher’s exact test ( p = 0.007). The increased risk of recurrent infection was associated with a history of diabetes (OR = 9.571; p = 0.013) and bacterial culture results showing mixed infection (OR = 8.75; p = 0.031). No significant associations were observed between other baseline characteristics and prosthesis-related mechanical failure. However, given the small number of events, these findings should be interpreted with caution. Discussion In this study, the most significant finding was that 90% of patients did not experience recurrence after receiving either single microporous titanium implantation or combined free flap treatment, with an average follow-up of 40.8 months. The postoperative 1-year VAS score significantly decreased from 7.2 ± 1.4 to 1.6 ± 0.7 ( p < 0.0001), and the LEFS score for the lower limbs increased from 28.5 ± 5.8 to a median score of 59.0 ( p < 0.0001). The implant integration was rated as “Excellent” in 86.3% of cases. Additionally, we found that a history of diabetes and mixed bacterial infections may be important risk factors for recurrent infections. Over the past few decades, both the Masquelet and Ilizarov techniques have been clinically applied as important treatment options for infected bone defects [ , ]. However, the effectiveness of these methods may be compromised by complications such as pin tract infections, donor site infections, non-union, mechanical issues, or even recurrent fractures [ , ]. Many patients are unable to bear weight during the early postoperative recovery period. For example, a previous clinical efficacy comparison analysis showed that the average fixation time for the Masquelet and Ilizarov groups was 10.15 months and 17.21 months, respectively, with the Masquelet group demonstrating better functional outcomes [ ]. For cases without soft tissue defects, our study showed a treatment success rate of 92.7% (51/55) in the single microporous titanium prosthesis implantation group, with complete weight-bearing achieved on average after 5.0 ± 0.7 months. Pain was significantly relieved at 3 months postoperatively and continued to improve until the last follow-up. This may be attributed to the protective role of complete soft tissue coverage on the prosthesis, preventing microbial colonization and mechanical stress concentration. For cases with soft tissue defects, despite more complex bone and soft tissue defects and reliance on microsurgical techniques for free flap coverage, a treatment success rate of 84.0% (21/25) was still achieved, which is consistent with previously reported success rates (82.3–96.5%) [ , ]. Postoperative pain and lower limb function continued to improve at 3 months and beyond, with full weight-bearing achieved at 5.8 ± 1.1 months. The core advantage of free flap combined reconstruction for infected bone defects with soft tissue loss lies in the vascular support provided by the free flap, which may further influence bone healing outcomes. Given the fundamental differences in baseline disease severity and soft tissue involvement between patients treated with single prosthesis implantation and those requiring combined free flap reconstruction, these subgroups were analyzed as distinct cohorts representing different tiers of reconstructive complexity rather than being directly compared for treatment superiority. Personalized free flap The results of this study demonstrate certain advantages over traditional treatment methods, such as the Masquelet technique. Chen et al. [ ] reported in a previous clinical study that the combination of 3D-printed microporous titanium implantation and the Masquelet technique for treating infected bone defects caused by osteomyelitis achieved a treatment success rate of 76.9% (10/13). They then preliminarily explored the efficacy of local pedicled flaps combined with 3D-printed microporous titanium implantation for treating tibial infected bone defects, with a treatment success rate of less than 60% (53.8%, 7/13 cases) [ ]. Notably, the incidence of flap-related complications in that study was 30.8%, which may have been due to poor blood supply and excessive tension at the flap margins. The second-stage prosthesis implantation surgery was performed on average 4.8 ± 1.4 months after the first-stage free flap transplantation surgery. Innovatively, we used a personalized free flap (free anterolateral thigh flap) for repairing complex and large soft tissue defects, while also expanding the bone defect area from lower limb to limb-wide infected bone defects. By implementing precise infection control strategies (vancomycin-loaded bone cement release + pathogen-guided antibiotic therapy), we further enhanced the therapeutic efficacy, and the study preliminarily verified the feasibility of staged treatment (first-stage infection control combined with flap repair of soft tissue defects, second-stage mechanical reconstruction) for complex infected bone defects. Although the anterolateral thigh flap was the preferred option in the present series, alternative free flaps may be indicated depending on the characteristics of the defect and patient-related factors. The latissimus dorsi flap provides a large volume of well-vascularized tissue and is suitable for extensive soft tissue defects [ ]. The radial forearm flap offers thin and pliable coverage for smaller defects requiring contour precision [ ]. The gracilis flap may be considered for moderate-sized defects when a shorter operative time and limited donor-site morbidity are desired [ ]. In selected cases, a free fibular flap can simultaneously address segmental bone loss and soft tissue defects, although its use may be limited in the setting of infection or compromised recipient vessels [ ]. Therefore, free flap selection should be individualized based on defect size, location, infection status, and reconstructive goals. Diabetes and recurrent infections Regarding postoperative complications, the overall complication rate was 10% (8/80), with recurrent infection (7.5%) and prosthesis and screw mechanical fractures (2.5%) being the most common. Among them, two diabetic patients with extensive dorsal foot soft tissue defects accompanied by large metatarsal bone defects both experienced recurrent infections postoperatively, and one diabetic patient had a recurrent tibial infection. Univariate logistic regression analysis showed that a history of diabetes was significantly associated with a higher risk of any complications and recurrent infection ( p < 0.05), which drew our attention to diabetic foot osteomyelitis. Previous studies have shown that in diabetic patients, the significant changes in ischemia and neuropathy are primarily in the foot, which greatly increases the risk of foot bone infection [ , ]. In response, our experience suggests that preoperative strict control of HbA1c (≤ 7.5%) and serum albumin ≥ 30 g/L should be prioritized. After microporous titanium implantation, we extended the antibiotic regimen to 8 weeks (instead of the usual 2 weeks) and used dynamic follow-up with infection markers to monitor recurrent infections. For the 3 cases of recurrent infection in diabetic patients, the medical team conducted detailed discussions and analyses, discovering that patients had not received standardized foot care after discharge, which may have contributed to the infection recurrence. Additionally, all three patients had varying degrees of peripheral vascular disease, which posed a challenge to flap survival and the growth environment. Therefore, we recommend that before surgical treatment of diabetic osteomyelitis patients, classification according to guidelines (high risk, low risk, or moderate risk), such as the DFU prevention and management guidelines published by the International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot (IWGDF) [ ], should be conducted to facilitate targeted, stratified treatment. Diabetes is known to impair immune function, microcirculation, and wound healing, which may contribute to persistent or recurrent infection [ ]. In our clinical practice, diabetes was not considered a contraindication to microporous titanium implantation or free flap reconstruction; however, these patients were managed as a high-risk subgroup. Management strategies included strict preoperative glycemic control, optimization of nutritional and metabolic status, thorough and staged debridement when necessary, and close postoperative surveillance for early signs of infection recurrence [ , ]. Multidisciplinary collaboration with endocrinologists and infected disease specialists was routinely employed. These measures may help mitigate infection-related risks in diabetic patients, although careful patient selection and individualized treatment planning remain essential. Moreover, Metaoy et al. [ ] found that local use of antibiotic-loaded implants can increase the eradication rate of infection in diabetic foot osteomyelitis and may further reduce amputation and mortality rates. Another meta-analysis showed that diabetic foot osteomyelitis patients treated with local antibiotic delivery systems had significantly higher healing rates compared to the control group [ ].

Another meta-analysis showed that diabetic foot osteomyelitis patients treated with local antibiotic delivery systems had significantly higher healing rates compared to the control group [ ]. In this regard, developing a local antibiotic delivery system on the surface of microporous titanium or modifying it for controlled drug release could be an effective strategy for treating diabetic foot infected bone defects. Nevertheless, the retrospective design of this study inevitably introduces the risk of selection bias and limits the ability to draw causal inferences. In contrast, a prospective study design would enable predefined inclusion criteria, standardized data collection, and uniform follow-up protocols, thereby improving data completeness and internal validity. Future prospective studies or registries are therefore warranted to further validate the clinical effectiveness and safety of 3D-printed microporous titanium prostheses in the management of infected bone defects. Additionally, from a clinical applicability perspective, several practical factors merit consideration, including cost, operative duration, and prosthesis manufacturing time. Patient-specific 3D-printed titanium prostheses generally involve higher upfront costs and require a manufacturing period for design and printing [ , ]. However, these factors may be balanced by potential clinical advantages, such as reduced need for staged reconstruction, earlier weight-bearing, and avoidance of prolonged external fixation in selected cases. Operative duration is primarily influenced by the extent of bone and soft tissue defects and the need for combined free flap reconstruction, rather than by prosthesis implantation alone. Future studies incorporating standardized cost-effectiveness and workflow analyses are needed to further define the role of this technique in routine clinical practice. Limitations This study has several limitations: (1) The retrospective design may introduce recall bias, and the lack of a control group (such as comparisons with traditional Masquelet or Ilizarov technique) may lead to selection bias. Future studies should include prospective randomized controlled trials to verify long-term efficacy while expanding the sample size; (2) The cases in this study are still concentrated in the early to mid-term follow-up, lacking long-term follow-up data beyond 10 years, which makes it difficult to assess prosthesis wear and the risk of late loosening; (3) A limitation of this study is the absence of a validated upper-extremity functional outcome measure, such as the DASH or QuickDASH questionnaire. This was primarily due to the very small number of upper-extremity cases in the combined free flap group ( n = 3), which would have rendered meaningful statistical analysis underpowered and potentially misleading. Future prospective studies with larger, multi-center cohorts are needed to allow balanced anatomical representation and comprehensive limb-specific functional evaluation (4). Risk factor exploration was based on univariate logistic regression only. Given the small number of events, multivariable modeling was not performed to avoid overfitting. Future studies with larger event numbers should apply multivariable regression to better control for confounding. Despite these limitations, this study represents the largest cohort of patients to date who underwent 3D-printed microporous titanium implantation or combined free flap repair and reconstruction for infected bone defects of the limbs, with or without soft tissue defects. The average follow-up of 40.8 months provides preliminary evidence for the feasibility and universality of personalized customization and staged treatment. In conclusion, 3D-printed microporous titanium prostheses (either alone or combined with free flaps) provide a reliable staged solution for limb infected bone defects. Throughout the follow-up period (≥ 3 months), both the single microporous titanium group and the free flap combined group maintained continuous improvements in pain relief and lower limb function. However, larger-sample and longer-term randomized controlled trials are still required in the future to validate the feasibility and safety of this surgical approach. documents.title: IWGDF guideline on the diagnosis and treatment of foot infection in persons with diabetes

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are among the most serious chronic complications of diabetes, with a lifetime incidence of up to 34% ( ) and an increasingly younger affected population. DFUs arise from the interplay of peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease (PAD), and impaired immune function, typically presenting as skin breakdown, infection, or tissue necrosis that may extend to bone or joints. These lesions markedly increase the risk of amputation—with reported rates up to 33%—and lead to disability in approximately 20% of patients ( , ), representing a major public health challenge. Once a DFU becomes infected, the resulting diabetic foot infection (DFI) usually begins with microbial colonization following disruption of the skin barrier and progresses under conditions of hyperglycemia, microvascular dysfunction, and impaired neutrophil activity ( ). Notably, the clinical manifestations of DFI may be masked by neuropathy, PAD, or immunosuppression; some patients develop deep tissue involvement or osteomyelitis without typical signs of inflammation ( , ). Thus, infection assessment should not rely solely on culture results but must integrate wound characteristics, systemic symptoms, and imaging evidence ( ). The severity of DFI is closely related to its anatomical spread. The foot’s fascial compartments facilitate proximal extension of infection along tendons and fascial planes. When inflammatory pressure increases within these closed spaces, ischemic necrosis may ensue, accelerating disease progression ( , ). Patients with chronic kidney disease, poorly controlled diabetes, or recurrent ulcers are at even higher risk for necrotizing or systemic infections ( ). Although many infections begin superficially, without timely intervention, they may rapidly invade deeper soft tissues, joints, or bone, posing a serious threat to limb and life ( ). Current international guidelines recommend staging DFIs based on infection extent, depth, and systemic involvement, and tailoring treatment accordingly—including antimicrobial therapy, debridement, revascularization, and multidisciplinary management ( ). However, large-scale, stratified clinical evidence on stage-based treatment of infected DFUs remains limited in China. To address this gap, we retrospectively analyzed 300 patients with DFU-associated infections using the IWGDF/IDSA classification system ( , ) to stratify infection severity, guide individualized treatment, and evaluate clinical outcomes. This study aims to provide evidence for standardized, stepwise management of DFIs, optimize treatment pathways, reduce amputation rates, and improve patient prognosis. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study design This was a single-center, retrospective observational cohort study. The study aimed to systematically evaluate the real-world application, microbiological characteristics, treatment response, and long-term clinical outcomes of a stage-based treatment strategy guided by the International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot/Infectious Diseases Society of America (IWGDF/IDSA) clinical classification system in patients with diabetic foot infection (DFI). The study protocol was designed and conducted in strict accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and received formal approval from the hospital’s Institutional Review Board prior to initiation (Approval No. 2019–701). As this study involved secondary analysis of existing, anonymized clinical data without new interventions, and all data collection and processing adhered to strict confidentiality agreements, the ethics committee granted a waiver for obtaining individual patient informed consent. However, all patients admitted to the hospital had signed a general consent form permitting the use of their de-identified medical data for retrospective medical research. 2.2 Study subjects and screening process 2.2.1 Study population and source The study population consisted of consecutive patients who presented to the hospital’s Department of Endocrinology and Metabolism, Vascular Surgery, and Wound Care Center between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2024 for diabetic foot ulcers (DFU) complicated by infection. (2) Quantitative thresholds: Isolates were considered clinically significant if they demonstrated growth above laboratory-defined thresholds (typically ≥10 4 CFU/g for tissue specimens) and were morphologically consistent on culture media. Conversely, organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus , Streptococcus species, Enterococcus species, Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa , and obligate anaerobes were consistently regarded as potential pathogens when isolated from appropriate specimens. (4) Repeat isolation: When available, consistent isolation of the same organism from multiple specimens or correlation with Gram stain findings (e.g., presence of neutrophils with intracellular bacteria) supported its designation as a true pathogen. All Staphylococcus aureus isolates were tested for methicillin resistance using both phenotypic and genotypic methods. The assessment was conducted within 24 h of admission by a multidisciplinary team comprising at least an endocrinologist, an infectious disease specialist, and a vascular surgeon. All team members received uniform training on the grading system. Grading was based on a complete history, physical examination, and preliminary laboratory and imaging findings, using the following specific criteria: Grade 2 (Mild) : Infection confined to the skin and subcutaneous tissue around the ulcer, with erythema extending <2 cm from the ulcer margin, and no clinical or imaging evidence of involvement of deep structures (e.g., fascia, muscle, tendon, joint, and bone). The patient has no systemic signs or symptoms of infection. Grade 3 (Moderate) : Infection is more extensive, manifested by erythema ≥2 cm from the ulcer margin, and/or infection involves the aforementioned deep tissues, but the patient does not exhibit systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). Grade 3(O) (Moderate with Osteomyelitis) : The criteria for Grade 3 infection were met, with a definitive diagnosis of osteomyelitis confirmed by imaging (magnetic resonance imaging or radionuclide bone scan) and/or a positive probe-to-bone test, but the patient still lacks SIRS. (2) Competing risk analysis (Fine-Gray model, death as competing event): To account for death as a competing event, we performed Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models to estimate the cumulative incidence function (CIF) for amputation across infection grades. In these models, death without prior amputation was treated as a competing event, while loss to follow-up was treated as censoring. The Fine-Gray model provides unbiased estimates of the actual probability of amputation over time, accounting for the fact that patients who die are no longer at risk. Cumulative event (healing) curves and cumulative survival (amputation-free survival) curves were plotted for each infection grade (2, 3, 3(O), 4), accompanied by 95% confidence intervals. The log-rank test was used to compare survival distributions between different grade groups. Univariate and multivariate Cox models were constructed to calculate hazard ratios and their 95% confidence intervals for different infection grades relative to the reference group (Grade 2), quantifying the magnitude of risk. The proportional hazards assumption of the models was verified by testing the correlation of Schoenfeld residuals with time. The outcome variable for nomogram development was the binary variable “non-healing within 6 months,” defined as failure to achieve complete epithelialization of the index ulcer within 24 weeks (168 days) from time zero. This definition encompassed two clinical scenarios: (1) patients whose ulcers remained unhealed at the 24-week follow-up assessment; and (2) patients who underwent amputation (minor or major) prior to achieving complete healing, as amputation precludes the possibility of ulcer healing. For patients who died within the 24-week follow-up period without prior amputation and without achieving healing, they were classified as non-healed in the primary analysis (worst-case scenario), with sensitivity analyses treating death as a competing event as described above. Patients who were lost to follow-up before 24 weeks without documented healing or amputation were excluded from the nomogram development cohort. Initial candidate predictors included all baseline clinical and laboratory variables associated with non-healing in univariate analyses ( p < 0.10). A multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression framework was used. Final independent predictors were selected via forward stepwise regression (based on the likelihood ratio test, with inclusion criteria p < 0.05 and exclusion criteria p > 0.10) to ensure a parsimonious and clinically usable model. Using the rms package in R, the regression coefficients of each predictor in the final Cox model were proportionally converted into a 0–100 point scoring system. The total score was then mapped to the predicted 6-month probability of non-healing, resulting in a visual nomogram. The concordance index and its 95% confidence interval were calculated for the model in the training set. A C-index closer to 1 indicates a better ability to discriminate between patients with different prognoses. A calibration curve was plotted. Patients were grouped into deciles based on their predicted risk. The mean predicted probability and the actual observed Kaplan–Meier estimated probability for each decile were calculated, and their agreement assessed. The Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test was also performed. Bootstrap resampling (1,000 repetitions) was used for internal validation of the model. The bootstrap-corrected C-index was calculated to reduce overfitting and provide a more objective estimate of the model’s expected performance on new data. To assess the robustness of our microbiological findings, we performed sensitivity analyses addressing culture-negative cases. We acknowledge that negative cultures, particularly in severe infections, may result from prior antibiotics, fastidious organisms, or sampling error. Rather than imputing a specific pathogen (e.g., Pseudomonas aeruginosa ) in all culture-negative cases—an approach lacking microbiological justification—we adopted a more conservative strategy. Based on the IWGDF/IDSA clinical classification system, 98 patients (32.7%) were classified as Grade 2 (mild), 126 patients (42.0%) as Grade 3 (moderate), 34 patients (11.3%) as Grade 3(O) (moderate with osteomyelitis), and 42 patients (14.0%) as Grade 4 (severe). Baseline characteristics across these groups are detailed in . A clear gradient of increasing patient vulnerability was observed with escalating infection severity. Patients with more severe infections were significantly older, had a longer duration of diabetes, and exhibited poorer glycemic control (higher HbA1c) (all p < 0.001). The prevalence of key systemic and vascular comorbidities—specifically hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and peripheral arterial disease—also increased significantly across the severity spectrum. In contrast, the prevalence of peripheral neuropathy was consistently high (>88%) across all groups. Detailed comparisons are presented below. 3.2 Microbiological characteristics Deep tissue cultures obtained after debridement were positive in 229 patients (76.3%). Gram-positive cocci accounted for 64.2% of isolates, with Staphylococcus aureus being the most frequently identified pathogen (41.5%, 95/229). Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) accounted for 45.3% (43/95) of S. aureus isolates. Gram-negative bacilli were isolated in 48.9% of cases, dominated by Escherichia coli (19.2%) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (12.2%). Notably, P. aeruginosa was markedly enriched in grade 4 infections (52.2%). Mixed infections involving ≥2 pathogens occurred in 38.4% (88/229) of patients and were significantly more common in grade 3(O) (69.2%) and grade 4 infections (60.9%) than in mild infections ( p < 0.001), suggesting increased microbial complexity in deep or systemic infections. Detailed microbiological profiles are shown in . Notably, the lower culture positivity rate in Grade 4 infections (54.8%) may partially reflect the higher likelihood of prior antibiotic exposure in this group, as these patients often presented with systemic illness and were more likely to have received empirical therapy before referral or before specimen collection. 3.3 Treatment and clinical outcomes All patients underwent standardized sharp debridement, with a mean of 3.2 ± 1.5 procedures. A total of 89 patients (29.7%) underwent revascularization, most of whom were in the grade 4 group (83.3%, 35/42). The initial empirical antibiotic regimen predominantly consisted of β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitors (62.0%). More severe infections (grades 3(O) and 4) required more frequent use of carbapenems (86.0% combined) and MRSA-targeted therapy (51.1% combined). Overall, infection control was achieved in 85.3% (256/300) of patients, but rates declined significantly with increasing infection severity ( p < 0.001). During a median follow-up of 12 weeks (IQR: 8–20 weeks), 204 patients (68.0%) achieved complete ulcer healing, with a markedly lower rate in grade 4 patients (33.3%, 14 of 42). This approach ensures that all patients contribute to the analysis for the duration they were at risk of healing. The median healing times reported, therefore, represent the time to healing among patients who healed, while accounting for the fact that some patients were censored due to amputation. In the training cohort, the model’s Concordance Index (C-index) was 0.82 (95% CI: 0.78–0.86), indicating good discriminative ability to effectively stratify patients with different prognoses. Following internal validation using the Bootstrap method (1,000 resamples), the corrected C-index was 0.80, suggesting good model robustness with low overfitting risk. The calibration curve ( ) showed good agreement between the model-predicted 6-month non-healing probability and the actual observed Kaplan–Meier estimated probability across the entire risk spectrum. The enrichment of P. aeruginosa in Grade 4 infections remained a significant association ( p < 0.001), and its presence was still correlated with poorer healing rates. 4 Discussion This retrospective analysis of 300 patients with DFIs provides a comprehensive, real-world validation of the IWGDF/IDSA classification system and underscores its critical role in guiding stage-specific, multidisciplinary management. Our data delineate a clear severity gradient: as infection progresses from Grade 2 to Grade 4, we observed a concomitant worsening of metabolic control (rising HbA1c), an increased burden of PAD, a shift in microbial ecology toward Gram-negative bacilli and polymicrobial infections, and a stark deterioration in clinical outcomes—particularly ulcer healing and limb salvage rates. These findings collectively affirm that the IWGDF/IDSA grade is not merely a descriptive label but a robust prognostic indicator that reflects the underlying pathophysiological interplay between host vulnerability, microbial virulence, and treatment complexity. Our study reaffirms the pivotal role of systemic and vascular health in DFI outcomes. Patients with severe (Grade 4) infections presented with significantly higher HbA1c levels (9.8% vs. 8.1% in Grade 2) and a greater prevalence of PAD (64.3% vs. 22.4%). This aligns with large cohort studies highlighting hyperglycemia-induced immune dysfunction (impaired neutrophil activity and cytokine dysregulation) and ischemia-driven impairment of antibiotic delivery and tissue repair as key drivers of infection persistence and progression ( , ). The independent association between lack of revascularization and ulcer non-healing (OR = 1.78) in our multivariate analysis reinforces the IWGDF principle that “revascularization should be considered whenever ischemia is present” ( ). Our subgroup analysis further quantifies this benefit: among PAD patients, revascularization was associated with a > 2.5-fold reduction in major amputation risk in Grade 4 infections (HR = 0.40). This underscores the necessity of early vascular assessment and intervention, particularly in moderate to severe infections. The observed shift in microbial profiles across grades—from predominantly Gram-positive cocci in mild infections ( S. aureus 66.7%) to Gram-negative bacilli (notably P. aeruginosa , 52.2%) and polymicrobial infections in severe cases—reflects both anatomical progression and prior healthcare exposure. Superficial ulcers are often colonized by skin flora, whereas deeper infections (fascia and bone) provide anaerobic niches conducive to Gram-negative and polymicrobial growth ( ). The high prevalence of P. aeruginosa and MRSA in Grade 4 patients likely also results from repeated hospitalizations and prior broad-spectrum antibiotic use, fostering selection of resistant organisms ( ). These findings support the current IDSA recommendation for broader empiric coverage (including anti-pseudomonal and anti-MRSA agents) in severe DFIs, especially in settings with high local resistance rates ( ). Notably, the “worst-case” sensitivity analysis confirmed the robustness of this microbiological trend, mitigating concerns about culture negativity in necrotic

Notably, all Gram-positive isolates remained susceptible to linezolid and vancomycin (100%), and Gram-negative isolates retained high susceptibility to piperacillin/tazobactam (89.3–95.5%) and carbapenems (93.3–97.7%) in the majority of cases, providing reassurance for current empiric regimens. However, the reduced susceptibility of Pseudomonas aeruginosa to ciprofloxacin (57.1%) suggests that fluoroquinolones should be used with caution as empirical monotherapy in severe infections. The designation of Grade 3(O) (moderate infection with osteomyelitis) proved clinically meaningful. Despite the absence of systemic inflammation, this subgroup exhibited outcomes markedly worse than Grade 3 and closer to Grade 4: healing rate 52.9% vs. 71.4%, amputation rate 47.1% vs. 15.9%. This aligns with evidence that osteomyelitis represents a unique therapeutic challenge due to poor bone vascularity, biofilm formation, and limited antibiotic penetration ( , ). In our cohort, Grade 3(O) patients required more aggressive debridement (mean 4.1 sessions) and prolonged antibiotics, yet nearly half underwent amputation. This validates the IWGDF’s decision to classify osteomyelitis separately and highlights the need for combined surgical (resection) and medical (prolonged, biofilm-active antibiotics) strategies, ideally within a multidisciplinary framework. Our treatment outcomes demonstrate a clear response gradient aligned with infection severity. Mild infections responded well to oral antibiotics and minimal debridement (96.9% infection control), whereas severe infections required aggressive surgical and pharmacological interventions, yet still faced high failure rates (38% uncontrolled infection, 66.7% amputation). This supports the “severity-guided therapy” approach endorsed by international guidelines ( , ). However, the persistently high amputation rate in revascularized Grade 4 patients suggests that when infection is complicated by extensive necrosis, multidrug-resistant organisms, or severe metabolic derangement, salvage may not be feasible despite maximal therapy. This echoes the “TIME-H” concept, where the confluence of tissue non-viability, infection, and metabolic hostility may render amputation the most appropriate outcome for patient survival and quality of life ( ). The development and internal validation of a nomogram for predicting 6-month non-healing risk (C-index 0.82) represents a step toward personalized DFI management. By integrating infection grade, PAD, HbA1c, and revascularization status, this tool quantifies individual risk and could help prioritize multidisciplinary resources to the highest-risk patients. Its performance remained robust in temporal validation (C-index 0.79), suggesting potential generalizability. Future integration of dynamic variables (e.g., serial biomarkers and imaging changes) and external validation in multi-center cohorts could further enhance its clinical utility. However, the review noted that all included studies had a high risk of bias, primarily due to insufficient events per variable, inadequate handling of missing data, and lack of internal validation. Their top-ranked predictors—multidrug-resistant infection, CRP, diabetes duration, troponin, and age—partially overlap with our factors (infection severity, glycemic control) while introducing novel biomarkers (troponin) that warrant further investigation. However, the complexity of machine learning models often limits clinical interpretability, a key advantage of our simple four-factor nomogram. Our nomogram offers several distinct contributions. First, it specifically addresses the 6-month non-healing risk rather than infection occurrence, antimicrobial need, or amputation alone, filling an important prognostic gap. Second, it incorporates the IWGDF/IDSA infection grade—a validated, internationally standardized measure—rather than Wagner grade alone, providing more nuanced infection severity assessment. Third, our model includes revascularization status as a modifiable predictor, directly informing treatment decisions. The C-index of 0.82 compares favorably with existing models (range 0.557–0.957) and remained robust in temporal validation (0.79), suggesting good generalizability despite the single-center design. Several limitations warrant consideration. First, the single-center, retrospective design may introduce selection bias and limit generalizability. Second, anaerobic and fungal cultures were not systematically performed. Given that anaerobes are present in up to 83.8% of DFIs when assessed by molecular methods and fungi in up to 31%, our microbiological profile likely underestimates the true microbial diversity, particularly in deep infections and osteomyelitis. This may have affected our ability to fully characterize polymicrobial infections and their impact on treatment outcomes. Third, microbiological data were dependent on specimen quality; the lower culture positivity in Grade 4 wounds (54.8%) may underestimate true pathogen diversity. Fourth, we did not assess biofilm burden or molecular resistance markers, which could provide deeper insights into treatment failure. Fifth, the microbiological findings should be interpreted with caution due to the retrospective nature of specimen collection. Although we attempted to obtain deep tissue cultures prior to antibiotic therapy whenever possible, a substantial proportion of patients, particularly those with severe (Grade 4) infections, had received antibiotics prior to admission or required immediate empirical therapy that precluded pre-treatment sampling. This may have led to an underestimation of true pathogen diversity, particularly for fastidious organisms, and may have contributed to the lower culture positivity rate observed in Grade 4 infections (54.8%). Prospective studies with standardized pre-treatment sampling protocols are needed to confirm the pathogen shifts observed in this study. Sixth, we did not assess the biofilm-forming capacity of isolated pathogens, which is increasingly recognized as a critical virulence factor in diabetic foot infections. Biofilms are present in up to 60% of chronic wounds and have been identified in 53.6–71% of DFU isolates. The presence of biofilms complicates treatment by reducing antibiotic penetration, promoting horizontal gene transfer of resistance determinants, and enabling bacterial persistence despite appropriate antimicrobial therapy. This omission may partially explain the high treatment failure rates observed in our cohort, particularly in polymicrobial and severe infections, and limits our ability to fully characterize the microbiological determinants of poor outcomes. Future prospective studies should incorporate systematic biofilm assessment using standardized methods (e.g., tissue culture plate method, confocal microscopy, or molecular detection of biofilm-associated genes) to better understand the contribution of biofilm formation to treatment response and limb salvage. Finally, while we adjusted for key confounders, unmeasured factors (e.g., nutritional status and social support) may influence outcomes. 5 Conclusion In summary, this large cohort study reinforces the clinical and prognostic validity of the IWGDF/IDSA classification for diabetic foot infections. It demonstrates that infection severity is inextricably linked to host metabolic and vascular health, microbial ecology, and therapeutic outcomes. Our findings advocate for a stratified, multidisciplinary management protocol: early revascularization for ischemic wounds, culture-guided antimicrobial therapy with consideration of resistant organisms in severe cases, and aggressive combined surgical-medical strategies for osteomyelitis. The developed nomogram offers a practical tool for individualized risk assessment. Future prospective studies integrating molecular diagnostics and dynamic biomarkers are needed to further refine management and improve limb salvage in this complex patient population.
